note_tweet.text:
How do we run a 145B model on a laptop or consumer GPU?

The short answer: we don't keep all 145B parameters on the GPU at once.

Edge0-145B is a sparse MoE model with 512 experts per layer. Only 10 are activated for each token, which works out to roughly 6.6B active parameters.

The key is our latent MoE architecture.

Attention operates at the full width of 2560. Before a token reaches the experts, a shared projection compresses it to 1792 dimensions. Another projection expands it back afterward.

This means the experts themselves can stay small, about 1.6 MB each.

We keep a few thousand frequently used experts on the GPU and stream the rest from system RAM as needed. So GPU memory usage depends largely on how many experts we keep loaded, rather than the model's full parameter count.

The model is also trained natively in 4-bit, with a built-in draft head to speed up decoding.

Local vibe coding #4: PCB design

This time we gave Edge0-145B a different task: design a circuit board, then animate how it gets made.

It placed the components and routed both layers in KiCad, brought the board into Unreal Engine 5, set up the cameras and lighting, and rendered a fabrication and assembly animation.

PCB design and 3D animation are usually two separate workflows, often handled by different people. Here, one model handled both on a single machine.

And none of the schematics or layouts had to leave the device.

For hardware teams working with sensitive designs, that last part matters a lot.

note_tweet.text:
How it learns to sound human:

TTS is usually trained on two things: the right words (WER) and the right voice (similarity).

But neither captures rhythm, pauses, or timing.

So we trained a realism critic that scores each output against a real person saying the same sentence in the same voice—ranked via a blind listening study.

Then: SFT → GRPO on accuracy + similarity → GRPO on the critic.

That last stage only saw Chinese and English prompts, yet it improved all 13 lower-resource languages.
